options.why: 5 bits represent only 32 different values.
Correct. 5 bits give only 32 values, but 6 bits give 64, which is enough.
Fewer bits are enough.
n bits give 2 to the n values, not 2n.

questions.explanation: Find the smallest n with 2 to the n at least 39: 2^5 = 32 is too small and 2^6 = 64 is enough.

questions.stem:
The following code segment is intended to display the sum of the values in `nums`.

```text
FOR EACH n IN nums
{
   total ← 0
   total ← total + n
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed when `nums` is `[15, 12, 15, 19]`, and why?

options.text: 15, because the loop stops after one pass
options.why: FOR EACH visits every element.

options.text: 0, because total is reset after the loop
options.why: The reset happens before the addition in each pass.
total is set back to 0 before each addition.

options.text: 19, because total is reset to 0 on every pass
options.why: Correct. The reset inside the loop discards the earlier values.

questions.explanation: Each pass sets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 19, remains. Moving `total ← 0` before the loop fixes it.

questions.stem:
Consider the following code segment.

```text
n ← 4
count ← 0
REPEAT UNTIL (n > 182)
{
   n ← n * 3 + 0
   count ← count + 1
}
DISPLAY (count)
DISPLAY (n)
```

What is displayed as a result of running the code segment?

options.why: n is updated in the last pass too.
The loop stops as soon as the condition is true.
The loop runs once more, because the condition is still false at that point.
Correct. The condition is checked before each pass, and the loop stops once n exceeds the limit.

questions.explanation: n takes the values 4, 12, 36, 108, 324; the loop body runs 4 times.

questions.stem: A hospital stores X-ray images that doctors use for diagnosis and wants to reduce storage space. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Lossless compression, because every detail must be recoverable
options.why: Correct. Medical images must be restored exactly.

options.text: Lossy compression, because the files become smallest
options.why: Losing detail could affect diagnosis.

options.text: No compression is possible for images
options.why: Images can be compressed.

options.text: Lossy compression, because it can be fully reversed
options.why: Lossy compression cannot be fully reversed.

questions.explanation: Medical images must be restored exactly.

questions.stem: A program has 4 independent tasks that take 38, 43, 48, 44 seconds. The tasks can run in parallel on two processors, and each task runs entirely on one processor. What is the minimum time to complete all the tasks?

options.why: The longest task cannot run at the same time as all the others on just two processors.
Correct. Split the tasks between the processors as evenly as possible; the time is the busier processor's total.
A better split exists.
That is the sequential time with one processor.

questions.explanation: The best split puts 87 seconds of work on one processor and 86 on the other, so all tasks finish in 87 seconds (speedup 1.99).

questions.stem: A network has computers P, Q, R, S, T, U. The direct connections are: P–T, Q–R, R–S, R–T, R–U, T–U. What is the minimum number of connections that must fail for computer R to be unable to communicate with computer S?

options.why: After that many failures a path still remains.
Correct. Removing 1 well-chosen connection separates R from S; removing fewer always leaves a path.
Some set of 1 connection already disconnects them.
Look for the fewest connections whose failure leaves no path.

questions.explanation: R has 4 connections and S has 1. Checking failures systematically shows that 1 is the fewest that leaves no path between them.

options.why: After that many failures a path still remains.
Correct. Removing 1 well-chosen connection separates S from P; removing fewer always leaves a path.
Some set of 1 connection already disconnects them.
Not every connection needs to fail.

questions.explanation: S has 2 connections and P has 1. Checking failures systematically shows that 1 is the fewest that leaves no path between them.

questions.title: Written response 1: program design, function and purpose

parts.prompt: Identify the expected users of the program and describe one way the program's design meets the needs of those users.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a specific group of users.
rubric.example: Home cooks preparing food for more people than a recipe serves.

rubric.criterion: Describes a design feature and connects it to a need of those users.
rubric.example: The program asks only for simple input (the user enters the ingredient amounts and how many batches they want) and gives a clear result (the program displays the new amount of each ingredient), which helps them let cooks make larger batches of a recipe without doing arithmetic by hand.

parts.prompt: Describe one input to the program and the output it produces. Explain how the output relates to the program's purpose.

rubric.criterion: Describes an input and the corresponding output.
Explains how the output serves the purpose.
rubric.example: The result shows the user the information they need to let cooks make larger batches of a recipe without doing arithmetic by hand.

parts.prompt: Describe how a programmer could use iterative or incremental development, including testing, while creating this program.

rubric.criterion: Describes building or refining the program in stages.
rubric.example: First write and test scale on its own with known lists, then add the input screen, then the display of results.

rubric.criterion: Describes testing with specific inputs and using the results to revise the program.
rubric.example: Test scale([0, 2], 2), which should give [0, 4], because the ELSE branch appends 0 for an amount that is not positive; if it does not, fix the procedure before adding features.

questions.title: Written response 2: algorithms, testing and abstraction

parts.prompt: (Algorithm development) Explain in detailed steps how the algorithm in `countPassing` uses sequencing, selection and iteration to produce its result.

rubric.example: The FOR EACH loop examines every score in the list.
The IF statement checks whether each score is at least the cutoff, and only then increases the count.

rubric.criterion: Describes how the steps in sequence produce the returned value.
rubric.example: The variables are initialized first, updated inside the loop, and the result is returned after the loop ends. For example, countPassing([81, 49, 46, 50, 82, 77], 70) returns 3.

parts.prompt: (Errors and testing) Describe a call to `countPassing` that tests a different condition than `countPassing([81, 49, 46, 50, 82, 77], 70)`. Identify the result the call should produce and explain why that test is useful.

rubric.criterion: Gives a specific call with different arguments.

rubric.example: 1, because 70 meets the cutoff (≥) and 69 does not

rubric.criterion: Explains what condition the test checks.
rubric.example: It checks a boundary or special case that a typical input does not, which could reveal an error the first test would miss.

parts.prompt: (Data and procedural abstraction) Explain how the list `scores` manages complexity in the program. Then explain how the parameters of `countPassing` make the procedure more useful.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the list manages complexity.
rubric.example: Without the list, each score would need its own variable, the number of quizzes would be fixed, and the count would need a separate IF statement per score.

rubric.criterion: Explains how parameters generalize the procedure.
rubric.example: Because the list and the threshold are parameters, the same procedure works for any data and setting, so it can be reused without copying code. To count failing quizzes instead, change the condition to s < cutoff.
